711322.t: Phono-semantic matching of Latin Rōma with ῥώμη (rhṓmē, “power, strength, might"”).

711350.t: From Biblical Hebrew שַׁבָּת (šabbāṯ, “Sabbath”), or, alternatively, from Aramaic שַׁבְּתָא (šabbəṯā, “Sabbath”).

711323.t: Of uncertain origin. Could be related to ῥώομαι (rhṓomai, “I dart”), as well as Sanskrit सार (sā́ra, “strength, power, energy”), which would hypothetically trace back to a Proto-Indo-European *serh₃- (“power; to move violently”).

711309.t: The term is likely related to ἔρυμαι (érūmai), with both forms showcasing different ablaut grades.

711312.t: By surface analysis, ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow, stream, gush”) + -σις (-sĭs). Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *srútis, from *srew- (“to flow, stream”) + *-tis.

711307.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hrutʰmós, corresponding to Proto-Indo-European *sru-dʰ-mo-s, ultimately from *srew- (“to flow”). Related to ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

711386.t: Disputed. The word is a widely-borrowed Mediterranean Kulturwort.

711321.t: Nominal formation from ῥώννυμι (rhṓnnumi, “to strengthen, be eager”), though others suggest a derivation from the possibly-related ῥώομαι (rhṓomai, “to dash, rush”) instead.

711366.t: From σάττω (sáttō, “to cram, to stuff”) and the suffix -μα (-ma). Possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *twenk- (“to press, squeeze”) (Proto-Germanic *þwangiz).

711365.t: Has been connected with Ancient Greek σάττω (sáttō, “to stuff, to press”), but this is semantically insufficient.

711381.t: The etymology is uncertain. Maybe related to σήθω (sḗthō, “to sift, bolt”) or perhaps a contamination of σαπρός (saprós, “rotten”) with an unknown word.

711311.t: Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *(s)rowpos (“accumulated filth”) and cognate with Proto-Slavic *strupъ (“scab”).

711324.t: From Proto-Indo-European *wroh₁ǵ-s, derivative of *wreh₁ǵ- (“to break, tear”), the same root of ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi, “to break”).

711308.t: According to Beekes, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *rewH- (“to draw”) and related to ἐρύω (erúō, “to draw, tear”), ῥυμός (rhumós, “pole of a chariot”) and ῥυτά (rhutá, “reins”).
